extracted.intended_audience: laboratory chemists and experimentalists performing pneumatic (gas) measurements and analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and standards for measuring, calibrating, correcting and analysing volumes and weights of gases in laboratory pneumatic chemistry using cloches, gasometers, eudiometers and weighing-balloons. Includes apparatus setup, identification tests, and pressure/temperature corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustable counterweight to equalize bell pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sliding weight (lentille 28 on tige 26 & 27) moved by a pinion and rack to adjust the lever DE so the bell A experiences equal effective pressure at all tilt positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move the weight along the rod to increase or decrease the corrective effect; because torque depends on lever length, sliding the weight permits compensating the loss of effective weight of the bell at all positions. Corrections need not be perfect — differences of a quarter to a half line are inconsequential in practice — but determinations for each pressure degree must be recorded orderly in a register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure gas quantities with a graduated arc (limbe) and nonius
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix a copper graduated arc (limbe lm) on the arc of the lever DE and read how much it descends using a fixed index terminated by a nonius giving hundredths of a degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the arc to convert lever motion into degrees (and fractions) to infer gas quantities; the nonius provides centesimal precision for small angular displacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate degrees-to-volume by filling known bottles
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many cubic inches correspond to each degree of the limbe by filling a bottle of known capacity (8–10 pints) inverted in the cuve and passing air until the bottle is full, then reading the limbe again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat with multiple bottles of different capacities and several trials; with time and careful attention one can 'jauger la cloche' for all positions. Use these repeated measures to compute the number of cubic inches per degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer well-turned, cylindrical cloches to minimise error
rubrics_metrics.description: A cloche should be well turned and truly cylindrical to avoid evaluation and calculation errors when measuring displaced water or graduations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture quality of the bell reduces systematic errors in volume determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for graduating cloches (marking volume graduations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill the cloche with air from a standard bottle of known volume (standard = 10 cubic inches), add successive measures of air and mark the water level each time until all water is displaced; then engrave graduations with a diamond point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep bottle and cloche at the same temperature as the cuve water; avoid touching the cloche (to prevent heating), cool it with cuve water if needed. For mercury tubes, use a bottle whose mercury weight equals one cubic inch as the standard and divide by inch or tenths. Use a diamond-tipped stylus mounted in iron to trace graduations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate volume determination by weighing displaced water
rubrics_metrics.description: After transferring the gas, invert the cloche and pour water in up to the marks EF and weigh that water to deduce gas volume from the mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conversion that one cubic foot (1728 cubic inches) of water weighs 70 livres; consult the tables provided for direct reductions. This method requires additional corrections for differences of fluid level inside vs outside the cloche (see §V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple, opposed reference marks to avoid level uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Place at least three or four small paper bands around the cloche at the water (or mercury) height to avoid uncertainty about the liquid level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varnish the paper marks once dry so they withstand immersion; this helps when moving the cloche between baths and avoids losing the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary identification by water absorption tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a very small known volume (e.g., one cubic inch) of water beneath a cloche containing gas mixture to observe immediate absorption behaviour and thus detect certain gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate, large absorption indicates gas like muriatic (HCl) or sulphurous acid (SO2); a very slight absorption approximately equal to the water's own volume suggests carbonic acid (CO2). Follow up with caustic alkali: CO2 is absorbed slowly and will be removed by potash solution over hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flame/combustion and oxygen-mixing tests for gas identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a lit candle into a jar of the gas: if the candle remains alight it's oxygen-rich; if it extinguishes it's mainly nitrogen; if the gas burns with a white flame when the candle is introduced it indicates hydrogen; a blue flame indicates a carbonated gas; loud detonation shows a hydrogen+oxygen mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing portions of the gas with oxygen and observing flame colour, vapours (e.g., red vapours and absorption indicating nitrous gas), or detonation behaviour helps identify components qualitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative separation methods for common gas mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: After preliminary identification, apply specific chemical or physical absorbers and volumetric operations: e.g., pass a known volume through potash/alkali to remove CO2; use sulfure de potasse solution to absorb oxygen in N2/O2 mixtures; use Volta eudiometer detonations to quantify hydrogen (by successive oxygen detonations and measuring volume decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For N2/O2 mixtures, leave the gas in contact with sulfure de potasse solution for days until oxygen is absorbed and only nitrogen remains; for hydrogen, add measured oxygen and detonate repeatedly until greatest volume reduction is achieved, accounting for water produced and any CO2 formed (which absorbs more slowly and can be removed by agitation). For nitrous gases, add oxygen and observe volume changes to estimate quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep full experimental notes: levels, barometer, thermometer
rubrics_metrics.description: Always record the difference of level (inside vs outside), the barometer reading and the thermometer degree for every experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quantities are necessary for later corrections of volume and weight to standard pressure and temperature; keep an orderly register of determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct volumes for atmospheric pressure (standardise to 28 inches Hg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because elastic fluids compress in inverse proportion to the weight compressing them, volumes must be reduced to a common pressure (28 inches of mercury) using proportional relations: volume1 : volume2 :: 1/pressure1 : 1/pressure2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert barometer readings from inches+lines to decimal inches (tables provided). Example formula and worked examples are given; use tables and logarithms to ease repeated calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for internal vs external fluid column differences (water/mercury)
rubrics_metrics.description: When gas is contained over mercury or water, the effective compressing pressure equals the barometer minus the difference of the fluid column heights (e.g., barometer − CE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heights of water columns must be converted to mercury-equivalent heights before arithmetic; use the given density ratio (mercury is 13.5681 times heavier than water) and conversion tables (table Nº V) to reduce inches/lines of water to equivalent inches of mercury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct volumes for temperature (standardise to 10°)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce measured volumes to the chosen standard temperature of 10 degrees because gases dilate/contract with temperature; adopt expansion coefficients (air ≈ 1/210 per degree; hydrogen ≈ 1/190 per degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the correction by dividing the measured (pressure-corrected) volume by 210 and multiplying by the degrees difference from 10; subtract the correction if temperature >10°, add if <10°. Use tables/logarithms to simplify repeated work. Aim to operate as close to 10° as possible to minimize errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined correction workflow (example/calculation model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply pressure correction (including subtracting inside-outside fluid column equivalent) to get volume at 28 inches, then apply temperature correction to reduce to 10°, following the proportional formulas and using provided tables for lines→decimal conversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides a full worked example (combustion of phosphorus) demonstrating stepwise calculation to obtain corrected volumes before and after combustion and deduce volume absorbed. Use the example as a model for similar corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine absolute weight of gases by evacuated balloon method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a large balloon (≈½ cubic foot) screwed to a plate with a valve. Determine balloon capacity by filling with water and weighing; evacuate and weigh the evacuated balloon; transfer gas from a cloche into the balloon (with valves opened) while ensuring internal and external water levels coincide; then reweigh to find gas mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for height of the barometer and thermometer to reduce the measured weight to standard conditions; account for residual air left in the balloon after evacuation (estimate from the height at which the test barometer stood during evacuation). Multiply measured weight appropriately (1728× etc.) to obtain weight per cubic foot. Dry the balloon by evacuation cycles before use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure thermal stability and dryness of apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain constant temperature for bottle, cloche and cuve during graduations and transfers; avoid holding the cloche with hands; dry vessels by evacuation and repeated use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the cloche is warmed by handling, cool it with cuve water. Dry the balloon by one or two vacuum cycles. Thermal disturbances introduce significant errors, so minimising temperature gradients is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat experiments, verify with multiple methods and be prepared to change approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Gas analysis often requires multiple, complementary operations; the art of gas analysis consists in trying different agents and methods until one is sure of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternative determinations (graduated bell, weighing displaced water, weighing gas in balloon) for cross-checks; if separation is uncertain, redesign the experiment, introduce new reagents, or use different apparatus until confident of separation and quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental construction/choice details that affect measurement quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose suspension chains and fixtures that do not elongate under load (chain of iron plates ikm), use three-branched stirrups for vertical suspension, and reduce friction at contacts with rollers and a band of rock crystal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a non-elastic plate-chain for the bell suspension to avoid length changes with load; employ rollers and a crystal band under contacts to reduce friction and improve sensitivity and repeatability of the balance/gasometer.
